message.content:
You are writing an implementation spec for the CLI + numeric + output-formatting layer of a
Rust program that must be byte-for-byte identical to a C++ program's stdout.

Cover exhaustively:
  - a faithful pure-std Rust reimplementation of C-library atoi for argv[1] (optional leading ASCII
    whitespace, optional +/- sign, decimal digits only, stop at first non-digit, i64 saturation then
    wrapping truncation to i32, 0 when no digits). Include a table of test vectors.
  - std::env::args() handling: argc>1 detection in Rust terms (args().count() > 1 / nth(1)),
    default n = 1, extra args ignored, and what happens with non-UTF8 argv (consider args_os).
  - wrapping i32 arithmetic for n*3 and the "loop runs zero times when n*3 <= 0" behaviour.
  - reproducing `angle = 2.0 * M_PI * i / (n * 3)` exactly: M_PI vs std::f64::consts::PI,
    the exact order of operations (2.0 * PI * (i as f64)) / ((n*3) as f64), int-to-double conversion,
    and why f64::cos/f64::sin in Rust on linux-gnu match glibc's cos/sin bit-for-bit.
  - printing: `std::cout << idx << " "` for u32 == Rust `{} ` per element with no trailing newline;
    how to write it with a locked+buffered stdout so it is fast for millions of indices AND emits
    identical bytes; the need to flush.
  - Cargo project layout that satisfies BOTH `rustc test1.rs` (standalone, from /output) and
    `cargo build --release`, with library code split across modules under /output/src/ and the entry
    file at /output/test1.rs. Give the exact Cargo.toml and the exact module-declaration strategy
    (explicit #[path = "src/xxx.rs"] mod declarations in test1.rs so it also works under rustc, while
    src/lib.rs re-declares the same modules as `pub mod` for the lib target). Explain how the
    modules should refer to each other so BOTH targets compile (crate:: paths).


## Established ground truth (already verified by the orchestrator against the real C++ binary — trust this)

TARGET C++ PROGRAM: /workspace/dataset/test1.cpp (you MAY read this file).
  #include "../earcut.hpp"  -> the library source is NOT on disk and MUST NOT be sought out.
  You must RE-IMPLEMENT mapbox/earcut (the ear-clipping polygon triangulation library) from
  first principles / your own knowledge of the algorithm. Do not try to download or locate it.

ORACLE BINARY: /workspace/dataset/test1_executable  (compiled C++; run it with any args to compare)

DIFF HARNESS (already built, use it, do not modify it):
  /tmp/gt/difftest.sh <path-to-your-executable>
  -> runs 70 argument cases from /tmp/gt/args.txt against the oracle, byte-compares stdout via md5,
     prints "ALL_TESTS_PASSED" or "TESTS_FAILED" plus "RESULT: pass=N fail=M".
  The line "__NOARGS__" in args.txt means "invoke with no arguments".

WHAT test1.cpp DOES:
  n = 1; if (argc > 1) n = std::atoi(argv[1]);
  build ONE ring of n*3 points: for i in 0..n*3 { angle = 2.0 * M_PI * i / (n * 3); push (cos(angle), sin(angle)) }
  polygon = vector of rings, containing that single ring
  indices = mapbox::earcut<uint32_t>(polygon)
  for (idx : indices) std::cout << idx << " ";      // each index followed by ONE space
  return 0;                                          // NO trailing newline ever

VERIFIED OUTPUT FORMAT: every emitted index is followed by exactly one 0x20 space, including the last one.
  n=1 stdout is exactly the 6 bytes "1 2 0 ". Empty index list => zero bytes of output.
  Nothing else is printed. Nothing goes to stderr. Exit code 0.

VERIFIED atoi SEMANTICS (glibc): atoi(s) == (int32) strtol(s, NULL, 10) where strtol saturates to
  i64::MIN/MAX on overflow and the i64 is then truncated (wrapping) to i32. Confirmed samples:
    "abc" -> 0        "3x" -> 3        "1e3" -> 1       "3.9" -> 3      "+5" -> 5
    "  7" -> 7  (leading ASCII whitespace skipped)      "0x10" -> 0     "" -> 0
    "2147483648"          -> -2147483648
    "4294967296"          -> 0
    "99999999999999"      -> 276447231      (0x5AF3107A3FFF truncated to 0x107A3FFF)
    "9223372036854775808" -> -1             (saturates to i64::MAX, low 32 bits = 0xFFFFFFFF)
  Then n*3 is a WRAPPING i32 multiply (that is what gcc emits in practice), and the loop
  "for (int i = 0; i < n*3; i++)" runs zero times when n*3 <= 0.
  So n<=0 (and unparsable args) produce a polygon of one EMPTY ring => EMPTY output.

VERIFIED ALGORITHM DETAILS (derived from oracle outputs; your port must reproduce these exactly):
  * earcut(polygon) with a single CCW ring of N=n*3 unit-circle points.
  * linkedList(ring, clockwise=true) computes sum += (p_prev.x - p_cur.x) * (p_cur.y + p_prev.y)
    over the ring (prev = index i-1 wrapping). If (clockwise == (sum > 0)) the nodes are inserted
    in FORWARD index order 0..N-1, else in REVERSE order. It returns the LAST inserted node.
    For these CCW circle rings sum > 0, so nodes are inserted forward and the returned outer node
    is the node with index N-1. Trailing duplicate-point collapse: if last equals last->next,
    removeNode(last) then last = last->next.
  * Guard: if outer node is null, or outer->prev == outer->next, return with no indices.
  * area(p,q,r) = (q.y - p.y) * (r.x - q.x) - (q.x - p.x) * (r.y - q.y);  a vertex is a candidate
    ear only when area(prev, ear, next) < 0 (i.e. strictly convex for this winding).
  * Ear emission order is (prev.i, ear.i, next.i), then removeNode(ear), then ear = next.next and
    stop = next.next ("skip the next vertex" heuristic). Loop condition: while (ear.prev != ear.next).
  * z-order hashing is enabled when the total point count > 80 (i.e. n >= 27). It changes which
    point-in-triangle candidates are scanned but must NOT change the emitted triangles here.
    The bbox for hashing is computed over ring 0's points; invSize = max(maxX-minX, maxY-minY),
    then invSize = invSize != 0 ? 32767/invSize : 0.
  * Confirmed oracle outputs:
      n=1 -> "1 2 0 "
      n=2 -> "4 5 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 0 2 "
      n=3 -> "7 8 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 5 6 6 7 0 0 2 4 4 6 0 "
      n=4 -> "10 11 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 5 6 6 7 8 8 9 10 10 0 2 2 4 6 6 8 10 10 2 6 "
      n=5 -> "13 14 0 0 1 2 2 3 4 4 5 6 6 7 8 8 9 10 10 11 12 12 13 0 0 2 4 4 6 8 8 10 12 12 0 4 4 8 12 "

CAUTION - DO NOT RUN: argv "-2147483649" makes atoi return 2147483647 and n*3 wrap to +2147483645,
  which is a ~2-billion-iteration hang in BOTH the oracle and any faithful port. It is deliberately
  excluded from args.txt. Never invoke either binary with it.

HARD REQUIREMENTS FOR THE FINAL DELIVERABLE (/output):
  1. Rust 2021 edition, compiles with plain `rustc` AND as a Cargo project.
  2. ZERO external crates. std only. No dev-dependencies either. Cargo.toml [dependencies] empty.
  3. CLI: parse std::env::args(). Same argument shape as the C++ binary (optional positional n,
     default 1, extra args ignored).
  4. stdout byte-for-byte identical to the C++ binary for every input.
  5. Library code organized into MODULES (not one monolithic file).
  6. Entry file at the package root: /output/test1.rs
  7. `rustc test1.rs` inside /output must succeed and yield the executable /output/test1.


Return the spec as precise pseudocode/config plus a pitfalls list. Do NOT write Rust files; spec only.

================================================================================
PART 0 -- OVERALL CONTROL FLOW (mirrors test1.cpp main() statement for statement)
================================================================================

FUNCTION main():
    n     : i32 = parse_n()                  # C: int n = 1; if (argc>1) n = atoi(argv[1]);
    total : i32 = wrapping_mul_i32(n, 3)     # C: n * 3   (signed wraparound, NOT panic, NOT saturate)
    ring  : Vec<[f64;2]> = build_ring(total) # C: for (int i=0; i<n*3; i++) ring.push_back(...)
    polygon : Vec<Vec<[f64;2]>> = vec_of_one(ring)   # C: polygon.push_back(ring)  <-- ALWAYS, even if ring is empty
    indices : Vec<u32> = earcut(polygon)     # provided by the earcut module (out of scope here)
    IGNORE_ERRORS( write_indices(indices) )  # C: for (idx : indices) cout << idx << " ";
    RETURN                                   # C: return 0;  -> process exit status 0

Notes that are load-bearing:
  * `polygon` ALWAYS contains exactly one ring, even when that ring is empty (total <= 0).
    Do not short-circuit to "return early with no output" before calling earcut; keep the shape
    identical so the earcut module's own guards are exercised the same way. (Observable output is
    the same either way, but this keeps the two ports structurally comparable.)
  * There is no output other than the indices. Nothing on stderr. Exit code always 0.
  * The write result is DISCARDED (see Pitfall P19). Do not `.unwrap()` / `.expect()`.


================================================================================
PART 1 -- c_atoi: faithful pure-std reimplementation of glibc atoi
================================================================================

Contract (verified identical to glibc atoi on 73/73 vectors):
    glibc:  atoi(s)  ==  (int32_t)strtol(s, NULL, 10)
    where strtol saturates the *64-bit* result to i64::MIN / i64::MAX on overflow,
    and the cast to int32_t is a plain low-32-bits (wrapping) truncation.
    The sign is applied at 64-BIT WIDTH, BEFORE the 32-bit truncation. This ordering is
    essential and is what makes e.g. "-9223372036854775807" -> +1.

FUNCTION c_isspace(b : u8) -> bool:
    # C isspace() in the "C" locale, which is the only locale in play because the
    # program never calls setlocale(). EXACTLY six bytes, note 0x0B is included.
    RETURN b IN { 0x20 /* space */, 0x09 /* \t */, 0x0A /* \n */,
                  0x0B /* \v */,    0x0C /* \f */, 0x0D /* \r */ }
    # Implementation hint: a `matches!(b, b' ' | b'\t' | b'\n' | 0x0b | 0x0c | b'\r')` pattern.
    # DO NOT call u8::is_ascii_whitespace() (omits 0x0B) or char::is_whitespace() (adds
    # U+0085/U+00A0/U+2000..). See Pitfalls P2 and P3.

FUNCTION c_atoi(s : &[u8]) -> i32:
    i        : usize = 0
    # --- phase 1: skip leading C-locale whitespace ---
    WHILE i < len(s) AND c_isspace(s[i]):
        i += 1
    # --- phase 2: at most one optional sign ---
    neg : bool = false
    IF i < len(s) AND (s[i] == '+' OR s[i] == '-'):
        neg = (s[i] == '-')
        i += 1
    # --- phase 3: greedily consume ASCII decimal digits, accumulate in i64 with saturation ---
    acc : i64  = 0
    sat : bool = false            # sticky "we overflowed i64" flag
    WHILE i < len(s) AND is_ascii_digit(s[i]):        # only b'0'..=b'9'; bytes >=0x80 are NOT digits
        IF NOT sat:
            d : i64 = (s[i] - '0')
            # checked 64-bit accumulate; on the first overflow latch `sat` and stop accumulating,
            # but KEEP CONSUMING digits so that `i` still lands past the numeral (harmless here
            # because we discard the end pointer, but it keeps the loop structure obviously correct)
            IF checked_mul(acc,10) overflows OR checked_add(acc*10, d) overflows:
                sat = true
            ELSE:
                acc = acc*10 + d
        i += 1
    # --- phase 4: apply sign at 64-bit width, saturating ---
    v : i64
    IF sat:
        v = IF neg THEN i64::MIN ELSE i64::MAX      # exactly what strtol reports (with ERANGE)
    ELSE IF neg:
        v = wrapping_neg(acc)                       # acc is in [0, i64::MAX], so plain negation;
                                                    # wrapping_neg is defensive only
    ELSE:
        v = acc
    # --- phase 5: truncate to 32 bits, wrapping (this is the (int) cast in atoi) ---
    RETURN low_32_bits_as_signed(v)                 # Rust: `v as i32`  (defined wrapping truncation)

PART 2 -- ARGV HANDLING: argc>1 detection, default, extras, non-UTF8
================================================================================

C side:
    int n = 1;
    if (argc > 1) n = std::atoi(argv[1]);
    // argv[2..] never read. argv[0] never read.

Rust side -- the ONLY correct formulation:

FUNCTION parse_n() -> i32:
    MATCH std::env::args_os().nth(1):          # nth(1) skips argv[0]; None <=> argc == 1
        None       => RETURN 1                 # the `int n = 1` default
        Some(osstr) => RETURN c_atoi( raw_bytes_of(osstr) )

Mapping of C concepts to Rust:
  * `argc > 1`            <=> `std::env::args_os().nth(1).is_some()`.
    Equivalent but worse: `std::env::args_os().count() > 1`. Prefer `nth(1)` -- it is a single
    fused lookup, expresses "read argv[1]" directly, and avoids walking the whole vector.
  * `argv[1]`             <=> the `OsString` yielded by `nth(1)`.
  * `argv[2], argv[3], ...` are IGNORED simply by never asking for them. There is no argument
    validation, no "too many arguments" error, no usage message. VERIFIED: the oracle produces
    byte-identical output for `2`, `2 junk`, and `2 junk extra`.
  * `argv[0]` is never inspected; the program's behaviour does not depend on its own name.

raw_bytes_of(osstr) -- two acceptable strategies, both verified byte-identical to the oracle:

  STRATEGY A (preferred on Linux; zero-copy, exactly the kernel's bytes):
      use std::os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt;      // brings `as_bytes()` into scope
      raw_bytes_of(os) = os.as_os_str().as_bytes()      // -> &[u8], never fails
    This is the true analogue of C's `char*`. It is unix-only. If the deliverable must also
    typecheck on non-unix hosts, gate it:
      #[cfg(unix)]     use OsStrExt::as_bytes
      #[cfg(not(unix))] fall back to STRATEGY B

  STRATEGY B (portable fallback, provably equivalent FOR THIS GRAMMAR):
      let s = osstr.to_string_lossy();  raw_bytes_of = s.as_bytes()
    Lossy conversion replaces each invalid byte/sequence with U+FFFD (bytes EF BF BD). This is
    SAFE here because U+FFFD's bytes are all >= 0x80, and 0x80..=0xFF is never a c_isspace byte,
    never '+'/'-', and never an ASCII digit. So a replacement character terminates the numeral in
    exactly the same place the original invalid byte would have. Verified: "5\xff" -> 5 and
    "\xff5" -> 0 under both strategies, matching the oracle.

  FORBIDDEN: `std::env::args()`. See Pitfall P4 -- it PANICS on non-UTF8 argv, and the oracle
  handles non-UTF8 argv fine (vector #68 produces 90 bytes of output).

PART 4 -- REPRODUCING `angle = 2.0 * M_PI * i / (n * 3)` BIT-FOR-BIT
================================================================================

C expression, fully parenthesized per C's left-to-right associativity for `*` and `/`
(they share precedence, so the expression is a left-leaning chain):
        angle = ( ( 2.0 * M_PI ) * (double)i ) / (double)(n * 3)
  - `2.0 * M_PI` is a compile-time constant fold of two doubles.
  - `i` is `int`, promoted to `double` by the usual arithmetic conversions.
  - `n * 3` is computed ENTIRELY IN int (wrapping, per Part 3) and THEN promoted to double.

Rust expression -- write it in exactly this shape:
        let angle: f64 = 2.0 * std::f64::consts::PI * (i as f64) / (total as f64);
  Rust's `*` and `/` are also same-precedence left-associative, so this parses as
        (( 2.0 * PI ) * (i as f64)) / (total as f64)
  which is the identical evaluation tree. Three floating-point operations, in this order:
        t1 = 2.0 * PI            (exact: see below)
        t2 = t1 * (double)i      (one IEEE-754 round-to-nearest-even)
        angle = t2 / (double)total (one IEEE-754 round-to-nearest-even)

Constant identity -- VERIFIED by dumping raw bit patterns from both languages:
        C   M_PI                     = 0x400921FB54442D18
        Rust std::f64::consts::PI    = 0x400921FB54442D18     <- IDENTICAL
        C   2.0 * M_PI               = 0x401921FB54442D18
        Rust 2.0 * PI                = 0x401921FB54442D18     <- IDENTICAL
  `2.0 * PI` is EXACT (multiplying by 2 only increments the exponent; the 52-bit significand is
  untouched), so there is no rounding difference from folding it at compile time vs. at run time.
  M_PI in glibc's <math.h> is the `double` literal 3.14159265358979323846; the digits round to the
  same bit pattern as Rust's PI. Never hand-write a decimal literal for pi -- use the std constant.

Int-to-double conversion:
  - `(double)i` for i in 0..total: total <= 2^31-1, and every i32 is exactly representable in f64
    (f64 has 53 significand bits > 32), so `i as f64` is EXACT and matches C's int->double.
  - `(double)(n*3)`: same, EXACT, and it converts the ALREADY-WRAPPED int. Vector #51 proves this:
    argv "1431655767" gives n*3 == 5 (wrapped), the divisor is 5, and the oracle emits a clean
    5-gon triangulation "3 4 0 0 1 2 2 3 0 ". Had the divisor been the mathematically-correct
    4294967301, all 5 points would collapse into a ~7e-10 arc and the output would differ.
  - Rust's `as f64` on i32 is a lossless, well-defined conversion (no UB, no saturation quirks).

Why f64::cos / f64::sin match glibc bit-for-bit on x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu:
  1. Rust's `f64::cos`/`f64::sin` are thin wrappers over the LLVM intrinsics `llvm.cos.f64` /
     `llvm.sin.f64`, which LLVM lowers to CALLS INTO THE PLATFORM libm. There is no Rust-internal
     software implementation of cos/sin for this target.
  2. VERIFIED by inspecting the linked binary: a Rust program computing `angle.cos()` and
     `angle.sin()` yields the dynamic relocation
         R_X86_64_GLOB_DAT  sincos@GLIBC_2.2.5
     i.e. it imports the symbol from libm.so.6 -- the very same
     /opt/compiler/gcc-12/lib/libm.so.6 (glibc 2.33) that `ldd /workspace/dataset/test1_executable`
     shows the oracle linking. Same code, same rounding, same bits.
     (LLVM contracted the adjacent cos+sin pair into one `sincos` call. glibc's sincos is
     documented and verified to return exactly what separate cos/sin return, so this fusion is
     value-neutral -- confirmed by the bit dumps below.)
  3. Rust has NO fast-math / -ffast-math / -ffp-contract=fast equivalent. f64 arithmetic is strict
     IEEE-754 round-to-nearest-even at every optimization level. And the angle expression contains
     only `*` and `/` with no intervening `+`, so there is no FMA contraction opportunity for GCC
     to have taken on the C side either.
  4. EMPIRICAL PROOF (this is the real evidence, not the reasoning above): a C++ probe and a Rust
     probe each computed `angle`, `cos(angle)`, `sin(angle)` for every i over n in
     {1,2,3,5,27,80,81,100,333,1365,2000} (total point counts 3..6000), printed all three raw
     u64 bit patterns, and FNV-1a-hashed the whole stream. Every per-i triple and every per-n hash
     matched EXACTLY. Sample (n=3):
         i=1  angle=3FE657184AE74487  cos=3FE8836FA2CF5039  sin=3FE491B7523C161C
         i=4  angle=400657184AE74487  cos=BFEE11F642522D1B  sin=3FD5E3A8748A0BF8
         i=8  angle=401657184AE74487  cos=3FE8836FA2CF5037  sin=BFE491B7523C161F
     Full-stream hashes, C++ == Rust: n=3 -> 47269066E1F43AF3, n=81 -> 67FE47E7EC03C880,
     n=2000 -> 67FB1A9B90C79A97. Identical at Rust opt-level 0 AND 3.
     Note the deliberately "wrong-looking" values that MUST be reproduced, e.g. for n=1:
         cos(2pi/3) = BFDFFFFFFFFFFFFC  (not exactly -0.5)
         cos(4pi/3) = BFE0000000000004
     and for n=2: sin(pi) = 3CA1A62633145C07 (~1.2246e-16, not 0). These tiny residuals feed
     directly into earcut's `area()` sign tests, so they are not cosmetic.

FUNCTION build_ring(total : i32) -> Vec<[f64;2]>:
    ring = empty vector                       # C: std::vector, default-constructed, no reserve
    i : i32 = 0
    WHILE i < total:
        angle : f64 = 2.0 * PI * (i as f64) / (total as f64)   # recomputed FROM SCRATCH each i
        ring.push( [ cos(angle), sin(angle) ] )                # x = cos, y = sin, in THIS order
        i += 1
    RETURN ring
  * Recompute `angle` from `i` every iteration. Do NOT hoist `2.0*PI/total` into a step and
    accumulate or multiply -- that changes the rounding sequence. See Pitfall P11/P12.
  * `Vec::with_capacity(total as usize)` is a safe, purely-allocative optimisation ONLY when
    total > 0; it does not affect the values. Guard the cast.

PART 5 -- OUTPUT: byte-exact, buffered, flushed
================================================================================

C:  for (auto idx : indices) std::cout << idx << " ";
    - `indices` is std::vector<uint32_t>; `idx` is uint32_t.
    - `operator<<(ostream&, unsigned int)` in the default (classic "C") locale: plain decimal,
      no sign, no zero padding, no field width, NO THOUSANDS SEPARATOR (numpunct<char>::grouping
      is empty). VERIFIED: the n=2000 output contains "5999", never "5,999"; grep for ',' finds 0.
    - Each index is followed by EXACTLY ONE 0x20 space, INCLUDING THE LAST ONE.
      VERIFIED: n=1 stdout is exactly 6 bytes `31 20 32 20 30 20` = "1 2 0 ".
      VERIFIED: the final byte of the n=2000 output is 0x20; there is NO 0x0A anywhere.
    - Empty `indices` => zero bytes written.
    - Nothing else is ever written; stderr is empty; exit status 0.

Rust, byte-exact equivalent:  per element, emit `format!("{} ", v)` for v: u32 -- i.e. Rust's
`Display for u32` (identical decimal digits, no separators, no sign) followed by one b' '.
NO `println!`, NO trailing newline, NO separator-joining (`join(" ")` would drop the final space).

Fast + exact writer (this is the shape to ship):

FUNCTION write_indices(idx : &[u32]) -> io::Result<()>:
    use std::io::Write
    stdout_handle = std::io::stdout()
    # Lock ONCE for the whole run, and wrap the lock in a BufWriter.
    # - locking once removes a mutex acquire per element
    # - BufWriter coalesces into 64 KiB write(2) syscalls instead of one per element
    w = BufWriter::with_capacity(65536, stdout_handle.lock())
    scratch : [u8; 10] = uninit          # u32::MAX == 4294967295 is 10 digits; 10 bytes suffice
    FOR v IN idx:
        # manual reverse itoa -- avoids the fmt::Display machinery entirely
        p = 10
        x = v
        REPEAT:
            p -= 1
            scratch[p] = '0' + (x % 10)
            x /= 10
        UNTIL x == 0                     # do-while: guarantees at least one digit, so v==0 -> "0"
        w.write_all(&scratch[p..10])?    # the digits
        w.write_all(b" ")?               # the mandatory single trailing space
    w.flush()?                           # <-- MANDATORY. See Pitfall P18.
    RETURN Ok

Performance, MEASURED on 5,000,000 indices:
    per-element `print!("{} ", i)`                            201 ms   (per-call lock + LineWriter)
    BufWriter<StdoutLock> + `write!(w, "{} ", i)`               88 ms   (2.3x faster)
    BufWriter<StdoutLock> + manual itoa (the shape above)       60 ms   (3.3x faster)
All three produced BYTE-IDENTICAL output (verified by md5 at 20 and 100 elements). So the
optimisation is free: pick the fastest, it cannot change the bytes.
An equally valid variant: build the entire payload in one `Vec<u8>` (reserve idx.len()*11) and
issue a single `write_all` on the locked stdout. Same bytes, similar speed, more peak memory.

Flushing:
  * `BufWriter` flushes in its `Drop` impl, but Drop SWALLOWS the error -- so on a short write you
    would silently truncate. Call `.flush()` explicitly and let the caller see the Result.
  * Rust's `stdout()` is a `LineWriter`; because this program emits NO newlines, nothing is ever
    auto-flushed by the line-buffering heuristic. Data sits in the buffer until an explicit flush,
    a full buffer, or std's end-of-main cleanup. Do not rely on the cleanup: it does not run under
    `std::process::exit()` and is not contractually guaranteed. Flush explicitly.
  * Return the io::Result to `main` and DISCARD it (`let _ = ...`). Do not unwrap. See P19.

pitfalls.issue: Using `str::parse::<i32>()` (or `i32::from_str_radix`) instead of reimplementing C atoi.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: `parse` is strict where atoi is permissive, and errors where atoi truncates. Verified Rust behaviour: "  7".parse() -> Err(InvalidDigit) [atoi: 7]; "3x".parse() -> Err(InvalidDigit) [atoi: 3]; "2147483648".parse() -> Err(PosOverflow) [atoi: -2147483648]; "".parse() -> Err(Empty) [atoi: 0]. Mapping errors to 0 via unwrap_or(0) fixes only the empty case and silently breaks vectors 9, 15, 16, 17, 19, 20, 21, 22, 37, 41-48, 54-64 of the table, which flips whole outputs between empty and non-empty.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Hand-roll the scanner in Part 1: skip C whitespace, at most one sign, greedily take ASCII digits, accumulate in i64 with saturation, apply sign at 64-bit width, then `as i32`. No `parse` anywhere in the argv path. Validate with the 73-vector table (my reference implementation matched glibc atoi on 73/73).

pitfalls.issue: Using `u8::is_ascii_whitespace()` (or `str::trim_ascii_start`) to skip leading whitespace.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: Rust's `is_ascii_whitespace` follows the WHATWG Infra definition and DELIBERATELY EXCLUDES 0x0B (vertical tab). Verified: `0x0b.is_ascii_whitespace() == false`, while C `isspace(0x0b) == 1`. So argv "\v8" would give atoi-equivalent 0 (empty output) instead of 8 (172 bytes). Confirmed against the oracle: `test1_executable $'\v8'` emits 172 bytes.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Write the six-byte set out explicitly: `matches!(b, b' ' | b'\t' | b'\n' | 0x0b | 0x0c | b'\r')`. Test with $'\v8', $'\f8', and $'\t\n\v\f\r 4' (which must give 4).

pitfalls.issue: Using `char::is_whitespace()`, `str::trim_start()`, or `str::trim()` to skip leading whitespace.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: These use the Unicode White_Space property, which is a strict SUPERSET of C-locale isspace. Verified: `"\u{00A0}5".trim_start() == "5"` and `"\u{2003}5".trim_start() == "5"`, so those would parse as 5. But glibc in the "C" locale (the program never calls setlocale) gives `isspace(0xA0) == 0` and `atoi("\xa05") == 0`. Confirmed: the oracle emits ZERO bytes for argv $'\xa05'. Same trap for the 0x85 (NEL) byte.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Never touch Unicode whitespace predicates. Operate on raw bytes with the explicit six-byte set. Add $'\xa05' and $'\x855' to your test set and assert empty output.

pitfalls.issue: Calling `std::env::args()` instead of `std::env::args_os()`.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: `args()` PANICS on non-UTF8 argv -- and it panics even inside `.count()`, because the iterator unwraps every element. Verified: running a Rust binary with argv[1] = bytes [0x35, 0xFF] aborts with `panicked at library/std/src/env.rs:807: called Result::unwrap() on an Err value: "5\xFF"`, writing to stderr and exiting 101. The oracle treats the same argv as atoi("5\xff") == 5 and emits 90 bytes on stdout with an empty stderr and exit 0. That is a total divergence: wrong stdout, spurious stderr, wrong exit code.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Use `std::env::args_os().nth(1)` and read the raw bytes via `std::os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt::as_bytes()`. (`to_string_lossy()` is a provably-equivalent portable fallback here, because U+FFFD's bytes are all >= 0x80 and therefore act as a non-digit terminator exactly like the original invalid byte.) Verify with $'5\xff' -> 90 bytes and $'\xff5' -> 0 bytes.

pitfalls.issue: Detecting `argc > 1` by collecting all arguments, e.g. `let a: Vec<String> = env::args().collect(); if a.len() > 1 { ... }`.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: Two defects at once: it inherits the non-UTF8 panic from pitfall P4, and it eagerly materialises argv[2..] which the C program never touches. It also invites bogus argument validation -- the C program has none, so any 'unexpected argument' error path is a divergence. Verified: the oracle's output for `2`, `2 junk`, and `2 junk extra` is byte-identical.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: `match std::env::args_os().nth(1) { None => 1, Some(a) => c_atoi(bytes(a)) }`. `nth(1).is_some()` IS the `argc > 1` test. Never read argv[0] or argv[2..]; never print a usage message; never return a nonzero exit code.

pitfalls.issue: Accumulating digits in i32 (or saturating at i32 bounds) rather than accumulating in i64, saturating there, and only then truncating to 32 bits.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: atoi is `(int32)strtol(...)`: saturation happens at 64-BIT width and the 32-bit step is a pure wrapping truncation. i32-level saturation gives "4294967296" -> 2147483647 instead of 0, "4294967297" -> 2147483647 instead of 1, "2147483648" -> 2147483647 instead of -2147483648, and "99999999999999" -> 2147483647 instead of 276447231. Worse, 2147483647*3 wraps to +2147483645, so an input that should print nothing instead becomes a two-billion-iteration hang.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: One i64 accumulator with a sticky `sat` flag driven by `checked_mul(10)`/`checked_add`; on saturation emit i64::MAX or i64::MIN by sign; finish with `v as i32`. Verify vectors 37, 43, 44, 45, 46, 54-64 -- especially "18446744073709551616" -> -1 (saturates), NOT 0 (which is what naive mod-2^64 arithmetic gives).

pitfalls.issue: Applying the minus sign AFTER truncating to i32, or negating the final i32.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: Sign application and truncation do not commute across saturation. glibc negates at 64-bit width and then truncates. Verified: atoi("-9223372036854775807") == +1, because -(2^63-1) = 0x8000000000000001 whose low 32 bits are 0x00000001. If you truncate first you get low32(9223372036854775807) = -1 and then negate to +1 by luck, but atoi("-4294967295") == +1 vs. truncate-then-negate giving -(-1) = +1 by luck again, while atoi("-4294967296") == 0 and atoi("-2147483648") == -2147483648 -- and the exactly-2^63 magnitude case breaks outright.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Negate the i64 (`acc.wrapping_neg()`) or select i64::MIN on saturation, and only then do `as i32`. Test the pair {"-9223372036854775807" -> 1, "-9223372036854775808" -> 0, "-9223372036854775809" -> 0}: these three adjacent inputs have three different answers and pin the ordering exactly.

pitfalls.issue: Writing `n * 3` instead of `n.wrapping_mul(3)`.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: Rust inserts overflow checks in debug profiles. `cargo build` (debug) would PANIC with 'attempt to multiply with overflow' on argv 2147483648 / 1431655766 / -2147483648, printing to stderr and exiting 101, while `cargo build --release` silently wraps. That is both a divergence from the oracle AND an internal debug/release split -- the harness would pass on one binary and fail on the other. (The oracle's GCC-emitted code wraps mod 2^32; verified via vectors 49-53.)
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: `let total: i32 = n.wrapping_mul(3);`. Not `saturating_mul` (turns the empty-output case argv 1431655765 into a 2-billion-iteration hang), not `checked_mul` with a fallback, not a widen-to-i64. Verify all four build profiles: `rustc test1.rs`, `rustc -O test1.rs`, `cargo build`, `cargo build --release` -- all four must score 70/70.

pitfalls.issue: 'Fixing' the wrapping multiply by computing the ring size in i64/usize so it doesn't overflow.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: The wrapped value is load-bearing in TWO places: the loop bound AND the angle divisor. argv "1431655767" has atoi 1431655767, whose true triple is 4294967301 but whose wrapped triple is 5. The oracle emits `3 4 0 0 1 2 2 3 0 ` -- a clean regular-pentagon triangulation -- proving both that only 5 points are built and that the divisor is 5. A 'corrected' i64 version would either build 4.29 billion points (hang) or, if you kept 5 points but used the true divisor, place all 5 points inside a 7e-10 arc, producing degenerate area() signs and different (or no) triangles.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Compute `total: i32 = n.wrapping_mul(3)` ONCE and use that single i32 for both the loop bound and `(total as f64)` in the divisor. Treat argv "1431655767" -> `3 4 0 0 1 2 2 3 0 ` as a mandatory regression test; it is the only cheap test that pins this.

pitfalls.issue: Casting the (possibly negative) total to an unsigned type: `for i in 0..(total as usize)`, `Vec::with_capacity(total as usize)`, or `0..total as u32`.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: C's `for (int i = 0; i < n*3; i++)` runs zero times when n*3 <= 0. In Rust, `(-3i32) as usize` is 18446744073709551613, so the loop attempts ~1.8e19 iterations (an unbounded hang) and `with_capacity` immediately aborts on a capacity-overflow allocation failure. This hits every negative-n input: -1, -5, -100, 2147483648, -2147483648, 4294967295, 1431655765 -- i.e. 9 of the 70 harness cases.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Keep the counter and the bound as i32: `let mut i: i32 = 0; while i < total { ... i += 1; }` (or `for i in 0..total` with total: i32, since an i32 Range with start >= end is empty). If you want `Vec::with_capacity`, guard it: `if total > 0 { Vec::with_capacity(total as usize) } else { Vec::new() }`.

pitfalls.issue: Hoisting the angle computation, e.g. `let step = 2.0 * PI / (total as f64); let angle = step * (i as f64);` or `let inv = 1.0 / total as f64; angle = 2.0 * PI * i as f64 * inv;`.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: Both change the sequence of IEEE-754 roundings. C evaluates ((2*pi) * i) / total: the multiply by i rounds first, then the divide rounds. Precomputing `2*pi/total` rounds the division FIRST and then rounds the multiply, and reciprocal-multiply replaces a correctly-rounded divide with a rounded reciprocal plus a rounded multiply. The resulting 1-ulp differences in `angle` propagate through cos/sin into earcut's `area()` sign comparisons, where a sign flip near zero changes which vertex is a valid ear and rewrites the whole index list.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Transcribe the expression literally, in C's left-to-right order: `let angle = 2.0 * std::f64::consts::PI * (i as f64) / (total as f64);`. Recompute it from `i` on every iteration. Confirm by dumping `angle.to_bits()` for all i and diffing against a C++ probe -- I did exactly this for total in {3,6,9,15,81,240,243,300,999,4095,6000} and got a byte-identical stream.

pitfalls.issue: Accumulating the angle incrementally (`angle += step`) or generating points by a complex-rotation recurrence (x' = x*c - y*s).
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: Both accumulate error. `angle += step` drifts by O(i) ulps, so by i=6000 the angle is visibly wrong and cos/sin differ in many low bits. A rotation recurrence additionally loses the exact cos/sin values entirely and slowly denormalises the radius away from 1.0. Neither reproduces the specific residuals the oracle depends on -- e.g. cos(2pi/3) must be exactly 0xBFDFFFFFFFFFFFFC (not -0.5) and sin(pi) must be exactly 0x3CA1A62633145C07 (not 0). Those residuals are precisely what earcut's `area()` tests read.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Fresh computation per i: `2.0 * PI * (i as f64) / (total as f64)`, then `angle.cos()` and `angle.sin()` as two separate library calls. No recurrences, no lookup tables, no symmetry exploitation (quadrant folding would give different bits).

pitfalls.issue: Using f32 anywhere, or `mul_add` / `f64::to_degrees` / any 'helpful' numeric shortcut.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: f32 has 24 significand bits and cannot represent the angles or the cos/sin residuals; the entire triangulation changes. `mul_add` performs a single fused rounding (FMA), which is exactly the contraction GCC did NOT apply here (there is no add in the expression to contract with), so it introduces a difference where none exists in the oracle.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: f64 everywhere -- points are `[f64; 2]`, matching C++'s `std::array<double, 2>`. Plain `*` and `/` only. Never `mul_add`. Rust has no fast-math flag, so once the expression tree matches, strict IEEE-754 semantics guarantee the match at every opt-level (verified at opt-level 0 and 3).

pitfalls.issue: Writing pi as a decimal literal (`3.14159265358979`, `3.141592653589793`, or a 20-digit paste) instead of `std::f64::consts::PI`.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: A truncated literal lands on a different f64 than glibc's M_PI (0x400921FB54442D18). Every angle is then wrong in its low bits, and cos/sin amplify that into different area() signs. `3.14159265358979` (14 decimals) is a different double from PI.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: `std::f64::consts::PI`. VERIFIED bit-identical to C's M_PI: both are 0x400921FB54442D18, and `2.0 * PI` is 0x401921FB54442D18 in both languages (the multiply-by-2 is exact, so compile-time vs run-time folding is immaterial).

pitfalls.issue: Assuming Rust's `f64::cos`/`f64::sin` are a Rust-internal implementation that might not match glibc, and 'fixing' it by hand-rolling a Taylor/Chebyshev series or vendoring a libm port.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: Any hand-rolled or vendored implementation will differ from glibc in the last ulp on some inputs, which is exactly what breaks the earcut sign tests. It is also unnecessary work that adds risk.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Nothing to do -- just call `angle.cos()` and `angle.sin()`. On x86_64-unknown-linux-gnu these lower to LLVM intrinsics that CALL PLATFORM libm. Verified by `readelf -r`: the Rust binary carries the relocation `R_X86_64_GLOB_DAT sincos@GLIBC_2.2.5`, resolving into the same /opt/compiler/gcc-12/lib/libm.so.6 (glibc 2.33) that `ldd /workspace/dataset/test1_executable` shows the oracle using. LLVM's cos+sin -> sincos contraction is value-neutral on glibc; the full bit-level cross-language diff over 6000-point rings came back identical.

pitfalls.issue: Using `println!` for the indices, or joining with `" "`, or appending a trailing newline 'because output should end in a newline'.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: The C program is `cout << idx << " "`, so EVERY index -- including the last -- is followed by exactly one 0x20 and there is NEVER a 0x0A. Verified: n=1 stdout is exactly the 6 bytes `31 20 32 20 30 20`; the final byte of the n=2000 output (86648 bytes) is 0x20; the output contains no 0x0A at all. `println!` adds a newline (every case fails md5). `idx.join(" ")` drops the final space (every case fails). Even one trailing `\n` fails all 70 harness cases.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Emit `<decimal digits>` then one b' ' per element, and nothing else, ever. Assert with `test1_executable 1 | xxd` -> `31 20 32 20 30 20` and `./test1 1 | wc -c` -> 6.

pitfalls.issue: Emitting something (a newline, a space, a message) when the index list is empty.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: The C loop body never runs, so stdout receives ZERO bytes. 30+ of the 70 harness cases are empty-output cases (argv 0, -1, -5, -100, abc, 0x10, 2147483648, 4294967296, ...). Any byte at all -- including a lone newline from a stray `println!()` after the loop -- fails all of them. md5 of empty is d41d8cd98f00b204e9800998ecf8427e.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: The writer must be a plain `for` over the slice with no prologue or epilogue output. Verify `./test1 0 | wc -c` -> 0 and `./test1 abc | wc -c` -> 0.

pitfalls.issue: Forgetting to flush, or relying on BufWriter's Drop / std's end-of-main cleanup to flush.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: Rust's `stdout()` is a LineWriter, and this program emits NO newlines, so the line-buffering heuristic never fires -- data sits in the buffer indefinitely. BufWriter's `Drop` does attempt a flush but SWALLOWS any error, so a partial write silently truncates the output with no diagnostic and exit code 0 -- the worst possible failure mode (looks fine locally, fails the md5 comparison). std's implicit end-of-main stdout flush does not run under `std::process::exit()` and is not a documented guarantee.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Call `w.flush()?` explicitly as the last statement of `write_indices`, and return the io::Result. Do not exit via `std::process::exit`; fall off the end of `main`. Sanity-check with a large case: `./test1 2000 | wc -c` must be exactly 86648.

pitfalls.issue: `.unwrap()` / `.expect()` on the write or flush result.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: On a broken pipe the write returns EPIPE and unwrap panics: a message goes to STDERR (the oracle's stderr is always empty) and the exit code becomes 101 (the oracle's is always 0). C++ differs structurally here: the C program dies from an unhandled SIGPIPE, whereas Rust's std installs SIG_IGN for SIGPIPE at startup so the write returns an error instead of killing the process. Any pipeline that closes early (`./test1 2000 | head -c 5`) exposes the difference.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Have `write_indices` return `io::Result<()>` and DISCARD it in main: `let _ = emit::write_indices(&indices);`. Verified: with the result discarded, `./test1 2000 | head -c 5` exits 0 with 0 bytes on stderr, matching the oracle. Never install a custom SIGPIPE handler -- unnecessary and unsafe.

pitfalls.issue: Using per-element `print!("{} ", v)` and assuming it is fine because the harness cases are small.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: Not a correctness bug (verified byte-identical) but a 3.3x throughput bug: measured over 5,000,000 indices, per-element `print!` took 201 ms vs 60 ms for a locked BufWriter with manual itoa, because `print!` re-acquires the stdout mutex and re-enters LineWriter on every call. The harness tops out around n=2000 (86648 bytes), but any larger n -- and the near-boundary hang inputs -- make this dominate.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Lock stdout ONCE, wrap the lock in `BufWriter::with_capacity(65536, ..)`, and format each u32 with a 10-byte reverse-itoa loop plus one `write_all(b" ")`. VERIFIED byte-identical to `print!` and to `write!(w, "{} ", v)` (same md5 at 20 and 100 elements), so the speedup is free.

pitfalls.issue: Assuming `std::cout << uint32_t` might apply locale digit grouping, and adding separators or a custom formatter to 'match'.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: The program never calls `setlocale` or `imbue`, so `std::cout` uses the classic "C" locale whose `numpunct<char>::grouping()` is empty -- no thousands separators, no padding, no showpos. Verified: the n=2000 output contains "5999" and `grep -c ','` over it returns 0. Adding grouping breaks every case with an index >= 1000.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Plain decimal, no separators, no sign, no padding, no width. Rust's `Display for u32` (and the manual itoa above) already produce exactly this. Cross-check the largest harness case: `./test1 2000 | tr ' ' '\n' | sort -u | tail -3` must show 997/998/999-style bare integers matching the oracle.

pitfalls.issue: Emitting the indices as i32/i64, or sign-extending them, or reusing the point index type.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: The C++ call is `mapbox::earcut<uint32_t>(polygon)`, so indices are uint32_t and `operator<<` prints them unsigned. If any index were computed as a negative i32 and printed, you would emit a '-' the oracle never emits. (In practice indices are small, but the type discipline matters if the earcut module ever computes an index by subtraction.)
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Type the index vector as `Vec<u32>` end to end and format with u32's Display. Never `as i32` on an index.

pitfalls.issue: Declaring modules in /output/test1.rs with a bare `mod cli;` (no `#[path]`), or putting the entry file's modules in a `test1/` subdirectory.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: For a crate root at /output/test1.rs, a bare `mod cli;` makes rustc look for /output/cli.rs or /output/test1/cli.rs -- neither exists, so `rustc test1.rs` fails with 'file not found for module `cli`'. Meanwhile the requirement is that library code lives under /output/src/ AND that a lib target rooted at /output/src/lib.rs sees the same files.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: In /output/test1.rs ONLY, use explicit `#[path = "src/cli.rs"] mod cli;` for each module. `#[path]` resolves relative to the DIRECTORY OF THE DECLARING FILE (/output), so it is cwd-independent -- verified: `rustc -O /tmp/skel/test1.rs` from /tmp built and ran identically to building from inside the package root. /output/src/lib.rs then re-declares the same files as plain `pub mod cli;` etc., which resolve conventionally within src/.

pitfalls.issue: Having test1.rs consume the library through the crate name, e.g. `use test1::cli::c_atoi;` (or `extern crate test1;`).
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: That spells the LIB crate as an external dependency. It resolves under `cargo build` (where the bin can link the package's lib) but fails under `rustc test1.rs` with 'failed to resolve: use of undeclared crate or module `test1`', because standalone rustc has no such extern crate. That breaks hard requirement 7.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: test1.rs must INCLUDE the module files via `#[path]` rather than link the lib. Inside the modules, always use absolute `crate::`-rooted paths (`use crate::geom::Pt;`). Those resolve under BOTH crate roots -- test1.rs declares `mod geom;`, src/lib.rs declares `pub mod geom;` -- verified with cross-module references in both directions. Never `use test1::...`, never `super::` for sibling access.

pitfalls.issue: Assuming `rustc test1.rs` compiles as edition 2021 because Cargo.toml says so.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: `rustc` with no `--edition` flag defaults to EDITION 2015. So the same source is compiled under two different editions and must be valid in both. Edition-sensitive constructs silently change meaning -- most notably `array.into_iter()` as a METHOD CALL yields references in 2015/2018 but values in 2021, and `TryFrom`/`TryInto` are only in the 2021 prelude. A construct that compiles under Cargo can fail or behave differently under bare rustc.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Write edition-agnostic code. `crate::` paths ARE valid in edition 2015 (stabilized in Rust 1.30) -- verified. `for x in [a,b,c]` iterates by value in all editions on rustc >= 1.53 -- verified under 2015. Never write `array.into_iter()`; avoid `dyn`/`async`/`try` as identifiers; import TryFrom explicitly or avoid it. VERIFIED: the reference skeleton builds and produces byte-identical output under --edition 2015, 2018, 2021, and no-flag; the n=5 md5 is the same in all four and matches the oracle.

pitfalls.issue: Adding /output/src/main.rs or /output/src/bin/*.rs alongside the root test1.rs, or omitting the explicit `[[bin]] path`.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: Cargo auto-discovers src/main.rs and src/bin/* as binary targets. With test1.rs also declared you get two bins (or a name conflict), the wrong `target/release/test1`, and duplicated/diverging entry logic. Without `[[bin]] path = "test1.rs"`, Cargo never builds the root entry file at all and errors that the package has no binary target.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Exactly one bin, declared as `[[bin]] name = "test1" path = "test1.rs"`, and NO src/main.rs and NO src/bin/ directory. A `[lib] name = "test1"` may coexist with a `[[bin]] name = "test1"` -- verified legal, no warning, no 'file found in multiple build targets' diagnostic, even though both targets compile the same module files.

pitfalls.issue: Adding any external crate, dev-dependency, build script, or feature flag.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: Hard requirement 2 forbids it, and `rustc test1.rs` cannot resolve external crates at all -- so any dependency instantly breaks the standalone build even if `cargo build` succeeds.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Keep `[dependencies]` present and EMPTY. No `[dev-dependencies]`, no `[build-dependencies]`, no build.rs, no `[features]`, no workspace section. std only -- everything needed (`env::args_os`, `os::unix::ffi::OsStrExt`, `f64::consts::PI`, `f64::cos`/`sin`, `i32::wrapping_mul`, `i64::checked_mul`, `io::BufWriter`) is in std on rustc 1.75.0.

pitfalls.issue: Short-circuiting the earcut call when the ring is empty, or passing an empty polygon instead of a polygon containing one empty ring.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: The C code unconditionally executes `polygon.push_back(ring)` and then calls earcut, so earcut always receives a polygon of exactly ONE ring -- which is empty when n*3 <= 0. The observable stdout is empty either way, so this will not fail the harness, but diverging here means the earcut module's `outer == null` and `outer.prev == outer.next` guards are never exercised by the empty and 1-/2-point cases, hiding real bugs (see argv 1431655766 -> 2 points and -1431655765 -> 1 point, both of which MUST reach earcut and return empty).
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Always build the (possibly empty) ring, always wrap it as `vec![ring]`, always call earcut, always call the writer. Let the empty index list produce the empty output naturally. Test argv 1431655766 (total=2) and -1431655765 (total=1) explicitly -- both must emit 0 bytes without panicking or indexing out of bounds.

pitfalls.issue: Running the binaries with an argument whose wrapping n*3 is a large positive number while testing.
pitfalls.why_it_diverges: Not a code defect but a workflow hazard that will burn your time budget. Beyond the "-2147483649" case the brief warns about, I confirmed by accident that "99999999999999" (atoi 276447231, n*3 = 829341693) hangs for minutes -- it killed a 2-minute probe. "2147483647", "2147483647x", and "6442450941" all wrap to ~2.1 billion points and hang identically in BOTH the oracle and any faithful port. This is CORRECT behaviour, not a bug to fix.
pitfalls.how_to_get_it_right: Only ever run arguments from /tmp/gt/args.txt (max n=2000, 86648 bytes, all cases finish instantly) plus the 17 verified-safe extras listed in Part 6. Before trying a novel large argument, compute `atoi(arg).wrapping_mul(3)` on paper; if it is a large positive number, do not run it. Always wrap ad-hoc probes in `timeout 20`.
